title: Standard method for microCT-based additive manufacturing quality control 4: Metal powder analysis
author: du Plessis, Sperling, et al.

steps.title: Load powder into container
steps.instruction: Place the metal powder directly into a small plastic cup (for particles 40–100 µm) or a thin plastic tube (for particles <40 µm) without any resin embedding.

substeps.instruction: For the larger powder cup, fill to a total powder width of approximately 2.5 mm.
For the smaller powder tube, fill to a total powder width of approximately 0.7 mm.
Fix the cup or tube on a precise glass rod and mount it as close as possible to the X‑ray source to minimise the source‑to‑sample distance.

steps.title: Perform dummy scan (optional)
steps.instruction: Run a short dummy scan before the real acquisition to let the powder settle, thermally stabilise the system and limit X‑ray spot drift.

steps.title: Configure scan parameters
steps.instruction: Set the microCT scanner according to the container size and desired resolution, applying the appropriate beam filter and spot size.

substeps.instruction: Select a voxel size of 1.5 µm for the cup (large particles) or 0.7 µm for the tube (small particles).
For the cup, install a 0.1 mm copper filter to prevent beam‑hardening artefacts; no filter is needed for the tube.
Set the X‑ray spot size to ≈2 µm for the cup; keep the spot ≤0.9 µm for the tube using system‑specific apertures.
Apply a very strong beam‑hardening correction during acquisition.
Enable detector shift to remove ring artefacts.
Average 2 images at each rotation step while discarding the first image.
Use up to 3000 rotation step positions for a full 360° scan.
Adjust the current to the maximum allowed for the chosen spot size and set the voltage as listed in Table 1.
Ensure the entire sample width fits the field of view; increase the X‑ray current to the system‑controlled maximum for best contrast.
If desired, first acquire a rapid low‑resolution scan at 10 µm voxel size to check for dense impurities before the high‑resolution scan.

steps.title: Run high‑resolution scan
steps.instruction: Acquire the scan for approximately 2–3 hours per sample at the chosen resolution (0.7–1.5 µm).

steps.title: Reconstruct and denoise data
steps.instruction: Reconstruct the raw projection data using a strong beam‑hardening correction and apply the default adaptive Gauss filter in VGStudio MAX 3.1.

steps.title: Visualise 3D and slice images
steps.instruction: Generate 3D surface renderings and cross‑sectional slice images in VGStudio MAX 3.1 to inspect particle morphology and internal porosity.

steps.title: Quantify closed porosity
steps.instruction: Segment closed pores only and compute their volume using VGStudio MAX 3.1.

substeps.instruction: Apply the “advanced surface determination” function with the auto setting, first with “remove all voids” enabled and then with it disabled.
Create an ROI from each of the two surface determinations.
Subtract the ROI obtained with “remove all voids” from the ROI obtained without it; the result contains only internal (closed) pores.
Run a custom defect‑mask porosity analysis on this ROI to obtain colour‑coded closed‑pore information.

steps.title: Analyse particle size and shape
steps.instruction: Perform particle size and sphericity analysis on the reconstructed volume using the foam‑structure analysis module in VGStudio MAX 3.1.

substeps.instruction: Select the material of interest and run the default analysis algorithm.
Accept the default “merge threshold” of 5 % for splitting touching particles; adjust this value if over‑ or under‑segmentation is observed.
Export the per‑particle data (volume, equivalent diameter, sphericity, etc.) to a CSV spreadsheet for statistical evaluation.

steps.title: Adjust resolution for small powders (if needed)
steps.instruction: If the initial 1 µm scan of a <40 µm powder gives poor contrast, repeat the scan using the smaller tube at 0.7 µm resolution to enable quantitative analysis.

description: Powder analysis is traditionally done using a laser diffraction method, such as described in ASTM B822 – 17. This laser diffraction method is simple, fast and provides estimated particle size distributions; however this is based on a spherical particle assumption. Often the particles found may be significantly non-spherical. Some studies have also made use of microscopy and image analysis to analyse the morphology of intact metal powder particles. However, the microscopy method can only provide pseudo-3D images, not true 3D images, hence only qualitative analysis is possible and internal porosity inside particles cannot be visualized. Sectioning of particles embedded in resin and imaging of these particles using a microscope is possible and has been used in combination with stereological image analysis to provide particle size distributions and shape information and in this case internal porosity may be visualized. However, this method has the disadvantage of being very time consuming and statistically challenging to calculate proper particle sizes, due to the sectioning of particles being inherently not through the middle in most cases. Another disadvantage with sectioning is that the sectioning process may smear over small pores and may therefore affect the images obtained. Metal powder analysis in AM has been applied to monitor changes in powder quality upon many cycles of re-use [1]. In this study it was shown that powder particles become less spherical and have an increasingly rougher surface with an increasing number of re-use cycles. It may also be that other types of powder partially fuse which can decrease powder bed flowability properties, but this has not been directly reported in the scientific literature to our knowledge. In any case the quality of re-used powder needs characterization to ensure maintenance of optimal properties.
